author: ribeye
dek: A Toledo dad embraced Meta's new wearable AI at Connect — mostly to settle a bar bet about Ohio State without ever touching his phone.
disclaimer: Parody: the Kowalski family of Toledo is fictional. The Meta Connect announcements are real, as reported by the Associated Press in September 2026.
headline: Toledo Man Buys Camera-Free Smart Glasses, Immediately Uses Them to Argue With an AI About the Buckeyes

ohio_quotes.quote: He bought glasses with no camera so nobody can film him, and now he talks to them all day. I married a man, and I got a man and his robot friend.

ohio_story: TOLEDO, Ohio — Ray Kowalski of Toledo did not need a new pair of glasses. He needed, in his words, "a witness." So when Meta announced a camera-free pair of Ray-Ban smart glasses that can talk back, Ray preordered the $349 Ray-Ban Meta Audio on the spot from his couch, telling his wife it was for hands-free directions to the Mud Hens game. By Thursday he was walking the Maumee riverfront asking the glasses — and, by extension, the AI agent Muse inside them — to settle the only question that mattered: whether the Buckeyes' backup quarterback should have stayed in the game last Saturday.

"I asked it who threw the interception, and it gave me the drive chart, the down and distance, and the weather," Ray said, standing outside Tony Packo's with a hot dog in one hand and his new glasses in the other. "Then I asked it if the call was stupid, and it said, and I quote, 'I can't make that judgment for you.' Coward. My brother-in-law from Perrysburg would have had an opinion in half a second." His wife, Denise, has already set a house rule: no asking the glasses anything during high-school football on Friday nights, after Ray spent the entire third quarter of the Whitmer game trying to get Muse to rank the top ten quarterbacks in Glass City history.

The Kowalskis' daughter, who is home from the University of Toledo for the weekend, has claimed the glasses for herself, mostly to have Muse plan her grocery run and read her the weather without her touching her phone. Ray, meanwhile, is already eyeing the next upgrade — the $1,300 VR Glasses coming next spring — and has begun the delicate work of explaining to Denise why a man who owns four pairs of regular glasses needs a pair that weighs less than a deck of cards. "It's not about the glasses," he said. "It's about the future. Also, the puck thing means I can watch the game courtside from my recliner, and nobody at Fifth Third Field can tell me to sit down."
real_summary: At its annual Connect conference in Menlo Park, California, on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026, Meta went all in on a consumer-friendly AI agent and AI-powered wearable devices. Chief executive Mark Zuckerberg opened his keynote by acknowledging it was a "wild time to be building," and said Meta remained optimistic because "we believe in people." Zuckerberg has distanced himself from rival companies' calls for a coordinated slowdown in advanced AI development, arguing that individual labs can ensure the technology is safe.

Meta said its recently launched AI agent, Muse, is the "centerpiece" of its vision for the future of AI. Unlike a chatbot, Muse can act on a person's behalf — planning travel, booking reservations, ordering groceries and completing other tasks — and Meta has partnered with companies including OpenTable, Spotify and Ticketmaster to help it do so. The company is working to bring Muse to its AI glasses lineup for hands-free access, and Zuckerberg said Meta plans to release a palm-sized keychain device called Muse Charm, packing in "the whole Muse experience," in time for the holidays in December.

The hardware announcements included Ray-Ban Meta Audio, a camera-free version of the company's smart glasses for listening to music, making calls and talking with an AI assistant, available in October starting at $349. The third-generation Ray-Ban Meta camera glasses are available now starting at $449, with a slimmer design and longer battery life. A hearing-enhancement feature turns supported glasses into an "FDA-cleared, over-the-counter hearing aid" for perceived mild to moderate hearing loss, launching in the U.S. later in 2026 for $150 or with a Meta One subscription. Meta's new VR Glasses, weighing about 100 grams — roughly a deck of cards, or about one-fifth of the Meta Quest 3 — will launch in the spring of 2027 and cost $1,300, using eye tracking and hand gestures instead of controllers.
source_note: AP reporting, Sep. 24, 2026: Meta Connect keynote, Muse AI agent, Ray-Ban Meta Audio and Gen 3 glasses, hearing enhancement, and Meta VR Glasses.
